My current finding is that for any \(n\ge2\) the unique “\(n\)-tastic’’ triangle satisfying the cyclic condition has  

\[
\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}= \frac{F_{n+2}}{F_{\,n-1}},
\]

where \(F_k\) is the \(k\)‑th Fibonacci number.  This was verified numerically for \(n=2,\dots,8\) (e.g. \(n=5\) gives \(13/3\), \(n=6\) gives \(21/5\), etc.) and the pattern holds exactly: the ratio equals the quotient of the side‑length \(BC=F_{n+2}\) and the incircle‑contact length \(BD=F_n\) shifted by one index.  Consequently  

\[
a_{2n}= \frac{F_{2n+2}}{F_{2n-1}}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{} \varphi^3=2+\sqrt5,
\]

so \(\alpha=2+\sqrt5\).  Hence \(p=2,\;q=5\) and \(\lfloor p^{q^p}\rfloor=2^{25}=33\,554\,432\), giving a remainder \(33\,554\,432\bmod 99991=57447\).

My current finding is that for even indices the “moderate‑size’’ solution of the cyclic condition (the one with the larger incircle radius) yields a ratio  

\[
R_{2n}= \frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
\]

that increases with \(n\) and appears to converge to  

\[
{\;2+\sqrt5\;}
\]

Indeed, numerical data give  

\[
R_{2}=3,\;R_{4}=4,\;R_{6}=4.2=\frac{21}{5},\;R_{8}=4.230769\ldots,\;R_{10}=4.235294\ldots,\;R_{12}=4.235955\ldots,
\]

which tend to \(2+\sqrt5\approx4.2360679\). The “tiny‑radius’’ solutions produce huge ratios (e.g. \(R_{8}\approx1.175\times10^{5}\)), but they correspond to \(K\) collapsing onto the contact point \(D\) and are therefore degenerate; the intended maximal value \(a_{2n}\) is taken from the non‑degenerate branch, giving the limit \(\alpha=2+\sqrt5\). Consequently \(p=2,\;q=5\).

My current finding is that for every admissible \(n\) the cyclic condition forces the ratio  
\[
\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}= \frac{F_{n+2}}{F_{\,n-1}},
\]  
so \(a_n=F_{n+2}/F_{n-1}\).  Consequently  
\(a_{2n}=F_{2n+2}/F_{2n-1}\to\varphi^{3}=2+\sqrt5\) as \(n\to\infty\); thus \(\alpha=2+\sqrt5\).  Using \(p=2,\;q=5\) we get \(\lfloor2^{5^{2}}\rfloor=2^{25}=33\,554\,432\) and \(33\,554\,432\bmod 99991=57447\).  This matches all numeric checks (e.g. for \(n=5\) the ratio is \(13/3\), for \(n=8\) it is \(55/13\)).

My current finding is that for any \(n\ge2\) the ratio in the definition of \(a_n\) is forced (by the cyclic condition \(KNK'B\)) to be  

\[
\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}= \frac{F_{n+2}}{F_{n-1}} .
\]

I verified this for the first several Fibonacci pairs \((d,e)=(F_n,F_{n+1})\):  

\((d,e)=(1,2)\Rightarrow a_2=3=F_4/F_1\);  
\((2,3)\Rightarrow a_3=5=F_5/F_2\);  
\((3,5)\Rightarrow a_4=4=F_6/F_3\);  
\((5,8)\Rightarrow a_5=13/3=F_7/F_4\); etc.  

Thus for even indices \(2n\),

\[
a_{2n}= \frac{F_{2n+2}}{F_{2n-1}}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\phi^3=2+\sqrt5 .
\]

Hence \(\alpha=2+\sqrt5\) (so \(p=2,\;q=5\)), and  

\[
\big\lfloor p^{\,q^{\,p}}\big\rfloor =2^{5^2}=2^{25}=33\,554\,432\equiv 57\,447\pmod{99\,991}.
\]
